newsitem.title: UK: UK opposition frontrunner offers party a veto.
newsitem.headline: UK opposition frontrunner offers party a veto.

text.p: William Hague, frontrunner in the battle to be leader of Britain's opposition Conservative party, pledged on Saturday to give party activists a veto over his appointment.

Opinion pollsters and bookmakers make Hague favourite in the six-horse race to replace former prime minister John Major, who announced his decision to step down after a crushing defeat in the election on May 1.
The Conservatives leader is currently chosen only by the party's members of parliament, unlike Britain's other major parties, Labour and the Liberal Democrats, who ballot their entire membership.
Hague, who at 36 years old is the youngest contender for the job, promised to change the procedure.

"I think the changes that we need in the party are so great and the task ahead of us is so demanding that I would not want to embark on that task without a clear expression of the wider support of the party," he told BBC Radio on Saturday.
He promised that if elected by the Conservative members of parliament -- a dispirited rump of just 164 -- he would speedily convene a meeting of the party's membership to confirm him in the job.
"At that conference, a ballot would be held at which I would seek a mandate and would not continue as leader without it," he said.
The fresh-faced and balding Hague, best known for a rousing speech to the party conference when just 16 years old, served as Welsh Secretary under Major.

The Conservatives, hit by a string of scandals and bitterly divided over Britain's role in Europe, face five tough years in opposition after suffering their worst election defeat since 1832, at the hands of the resurgent Labour Party.
But the six candidates bidding to be the man to take on Labour leader Tony Blair put their differences behind them on Saturday for a joint protest against Labour tax plans.
The six contenders -- from former finance minister Kenneth Clarke to rightwinger John Redwood -- took the highly unusual step of writing a joint letter to the London Times.
They warned that Labour's plan for a windfall tax on utility companies would hit ordinary customers, shareholders and employees.
The controversial tax is intended to raise up to five billion pounds ($8 billion) that will be used to get the young and long-term unemployed back to work.
"We do think that the proposed method is fraught with danger," the six said in their letter.
